sources.citation: Pogoson, Ohioma I. & Francis O. Egbokhare (eds.). 2002. New Perspectives in Edoid Studies: Essays in Honour of Ronald Peter Schaefer (CASAS Book Series 20). Cape Town: CASAS. 154 pp. scan, UI repository item 123456789/5455.
sources.note: Image-only scan; scanned table of contents: chapters on Edo history, Benin, Ora/Benin, Emai ideophones, Edo personal names, Edo nominalization -- no chapter on Sasaru or any Akoko-Edo NCE lect. Not relevant to Sasaru stress.

sources.citation: Rolle, Nicholas. 2026. Tone diachrony beyond tonogenesis: Reconstructing the tone melodies of nouns in Proto-Edoid (Niger-Congo). lingbuzz/009572 v3, forthcoming in Diachronica.
sources.note: Family-wide tone database from 40 sources on 21 Edoid languages; footnote: 'The Edoid languages not surveyed in this paper are Ikhin-Arokho, Enwan, Ikpeshi, Igwe, Sasaru [sxs], Iyayu, Akuku, and Okpe' -- confirms no tone-marked Sasaru source exists. Nothing on Sasaru stress.

Decker, Ken, John Muniru, David Onoja, Lewinan Andrew & Samuel Eju. 2024. A Sociolinguistic Profile of Five Southern Northwestern Edoid Languages in Southern Nigeria. Journal of Language Survey Reports 2024-012. SIL International.
sources.note: Sasaru [sxs] only in the glossary of neighbouring groups and in Akhukhu oral history ('fought with the Sasaru and Okpe people for land'); no Sasaru wordlist or phonology.

sources.citation: Blench, Roger. 2020 [ed. IV]. An Atlas of Nigerian Languages. Cambridge: Kay Williamson Educational Foundation.
sources.note: Entry 409 Sasaru-Enwan-Igwe: Akoko-Edo LGA, 3,775 (1952), North-Central Edoid ii, dialects Enwan, Igwe, Sasaru; 'Refs. Comparative: Elugbe (1989)' only -- no phonology or grammar reference exists.

sources.citation: Lewis, 'Demola. 2016. A Leipzig-Jakarta Vocabulary Reconstruction and Sound Correspondence based Sub-grouping of North Edoid. Abstract with appendix wordlists (16 pp.), 2nd International Congress 'Towards Proto-Niger-Congo: Comparison and Reconstruction', Paris (LLACAN/CNRS), 1-3 September 2016.
sources.note: No prose on prosody: the 2-page abstract treats segmental sound correspondences (prefix vowels, C1 kp~gw~w, nasal vowels) and ASJP subgrouping. The appendix gives ~100 Leipzig-Jakarta items for Sasaru in IPA with every syllable tone-marked (acute, grave and macron, i.e. three marked pitch levels), which is tone-marked WORDLIST data only -- it implies the transcriber treats Sasaru as a tone language but states nothing about the tone inventory or about stress.

sources.citation: Lewis, Demola. 2015. Deciphering Aborigines and Migrants from Cognation and Topography in North-Western Edo. Lengua y Migracion 7(1): 29-51.
sources.note: Nothing. Lexicostatistics only: Table 5 'Cognation percentages for Igwe Sale-Sasaru-Enwa', Sasaru 61% with Enwa; Sasaru = Owan migrants into Akoko-Edo, citing Lewis 2013:150-154. No tone or stress.

sources.citation: Lewis, Demola. 2015. Geography and Lexical Feature Diffusion in Northwestern Edo. USEM Journal of Languages, Linguistics and Literature (Department of Linguistics and Nigerian Languages, University of Uyo) 7: 124-147. ISSN 2141-4971.
sources.note: Areal-lexical study: numbered example sets give tone-marked phonetic forms for Sasaru (e.g. (1) 'sleep' Sasaru form on p.129, also 'feather', 'name', 'fight', 'road', 'neck', 'bite', 'dig', 'see', 'year' sets) grouped by diffusion zone. The words tone, stress, pitch, accent and syllable do not occur in the article; no phonology section. Tone marks on cited forms are wordlist-type data only, not a statement. (extracted text drops the phonetic font; forms verified visually on the rendered page.)

sources.citation: Egbokhare, Francis O. 2011. The Sound of Meaning. Inaugural lecture, University of Ibadan.
sources.note: Sasaru appears only in the list of villages where Northern Edo project tapes were recorded; Table 8 (tone systems 2 / 2+DS / 3 for NWE and NCE languages) has no Sasaru, Enwan or Igwe row. No stress statement.

sources.citation: Pogoson, O. & F. Egbokhare. 2002. Relevant linguistic and material evidential inferences and Edo histories. In New Perspectives in Edoid Studies, 16-33.
sources.note: History/classification essay (24 pp); watermark-only text; no Sasaru phonology.

sources.citation: Elugbe, Ben Ohi. 1989. Edoid. In J. Bendor-Samuel (ed.), The Niger-Congo Languages, 291-304. Lanham: UPA. (Zenodo 5618102)
sources.note: Igwe listed in NCE classification only; no Sasaru data; sec. 13.3.4 tone systems does not mention Sasaru/Enwan/Igwe; no stress statement.

sources.citation: Elugbe, Ben Ohiomamhe. 1989. Comparative Edoid: Phonology and Lexicon (Delta Series 6). Port Harcourt: University of Port Harcourt Press. xvii+253 pp. (Zenodo 5688969, CC-BY)
sources.note: Nothing for Sasaru. Sasaru is named only on pp.10-11 ('most likely North-Central Edoid peoples: Ososo, Ate, Ikpeshi, Sasaru, and Enwan, all of Akoko-Edo') and in the classification list p.24 '(h) Igwe-Enwa-Sasaru', 'left out of the family tree because their exact relationship with the rest of NCE has not been determined'. No Sasaru sketch in ch.4, no Sasaru forms in the lexicon; the word 'stress' occurs nowhere in the book.
